mappings.note: Iodine is added to boiled and to chewed rice and the colours recorded in a table: an investigation with a control and observations.
Reads the bottle-and-balloon model, balloons for lungs and rubber sheet for diaphragm, which is explaining the working of a model made from everyday materials.
Compares what atmospheric and exhaled air do to lime water: the observation step of the experiment.
Completes the mouth-to-anus sequence of the alimentary canal, which is the organ-system flow chart LO-121 names.
Three tubes, chapati, chewed chapati and boiled potato, with the iodine result predicted and reasoned for each: a designed comparison.
Matches nostrils, nasal passages, windpipe, alveoli and rib cage to what each does: parts identified by their function, which C-SCI1.1 lists as an observable feature.
Frames questions that separate breathing from respiration, which turns on knowing what each process is. Not LO-114, which covers materials and organisms rather than processes.
Chooses the most accurate statement about what we inhale, air rich in oxygen rather than oxygen alone: precision about the breathing process.
Sneezing in dusty air explained as a reflex that clears irritants: the response traced to its cause.

This row carries leftover sneezing text in the stem, but the options and answer are the breathing-against-respiration distinction, which is an explanation of the two processes. The stem leakage is reported as a defect.
Nostrils as the way air enters: identification of the part where the pathway starts.
Hairs and mucus trap dust before air reaches the lungs: what the part does within the process, so LO-118 rather than simple naming.
Names the windpipe as the tube to the lungs.
Names the alveoli as the air sacs where exchange happens.
The rib cage as the bony guard of the lungs: a part identified by position and role.
Ribs up and out with the diaphragm down during inhalation: the mechanism of breathing in.
Works out what Rakshita's two-tube lime water set-up is testing and how she could confirm it: reading and extending an investigation.
Names life processes as the collective category for nutrition, respiration, excretion and reproduction: a category named.
Picks bees sucking nectar as a way animals obtain food, which places a feeding habit among the varieties of animal nutrition.
Why complex food must be simplified before the body can use it: the purpose of digestion explained.
Names the alimentary canal as the tube from mouth to anus.
Why one runner breathes faster than the other after the same run: an observed difference traced to possible causes. Not LO-120, because the counting is given and only the explanation is wanted.
Identifies what Yadu's rice-flour and saliva tubes are testing, which is reading the purpose of an investigation from its design.
Stomach acid breaking down protein and killing bacteria: a step of the digestive process explained.
Mucus shielding the stomach lining from its own acid, another functional step of the process.
Beaumont observing digestion through St Martin's wound is a story of scientific discovery. Not LO-118, since the answer is what the case revealed rather than the mechanism itself.
Names the small intestine as the longest part of the canal: identification of an organ by a physical feature.
Names the liver and pancreas as the glands that pour juices into the small intestine.
Bile neutralising acid and emulsifying fat: what the secretion does in the process.
Pancreatic juice acting on all three food groups, another functional step.
Digestion beginning in the mouth: where the process starts rather than what the mouth is.
Names mechanical digestion as the physical breaking up of food, a stage of the process.
Saliva starting the chemical breakdown of starch: the chemical stage in the mouth.
Why chewed rice barely colours with iodine: the result traced to saliva having converted the starch. Not LO-116, because the experiment is given and only the cause is asked for.
Names digestion as the whole breaking-down process.
Names the oesophagus as the tube from mouth to stomach.
Peristalsis as the wave of muscular contraction that moves food along: the mechanism of transport.
Names egestion as the removal of undigested waste, the last stage of the process.
Gut bacteria breaking down fibre and making some nutrients: a functional part of digestion in the large intestine.
Rumination as bringing the cud back for more chewing, a digestive process described for ruminants.
